item.title: European-Japanese BepiColombo mission becomes 2nd ever to arrive in orbit around Mercury
item.description: null Update for 2:50 p.m. ET on Nov. 23: On Sunday afternoon (Nov. 22), the BepiColombo team announced that, while the spacecraft did successfully arrive in orbit around Mercury on Saturday (Nov. 21), the engine burn that got it there was cut short due to a software glitch. On Monday (Nov. 23), we got another update : BepiColombo "is safe and in a stable orbit around Mercury" and is on track for the next big milestone: The separation of its two orbiters on Dec. 9. For just the second time ever, Mercury has received a robotic visitor from Earth. The BepiColombo mission — a joint effort of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency ( JAXA ) — arrived in orbit around Mercury on Saturday (Nov. 21), more than eight years after leaving its home planet. Before BepiColombo, just one spacecraft had ever circled the solar system's innermost planet: NASA's MESSENGER , which did so from March 2011 to April 2015. BepiColombo consists of two main spacecraft: ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO), also known as Mio. The duo launched — along with a power and propulsion element called the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) — aboard an Ariane 5 rocket from French Guiana in October 2018 , beginning a long and looping trip through the inner solar system. Mercury is a difficult planet to reach because it's so close to the sun . Spacecraft approaching the planet are accelerated to high velocities by the immense gravitational pull of our star and must therefore shed a great deal of kinetic energy to be captured by Mercury's much weaker tug. So the BepiColombo team designed a trajectory that featured one flyby of Earth , two of Venus and six of Mercury over the course of about seven years. That flight time was increased by a year , however, after the mission suffered an issue with its solar panels, which reduced the power available for the MTM's electric thrusters. BepiColombo's arrival at Mercury will take a total of about six months. (Image credit: European Space Agency) Saturday's orbital insertion came after a 37-minute-long engine burn, which began at 1:24 p.m. EST (1824 GMT). There was a bit drama involved, however, as confirmation of the maneuver's success didn't come for several hours afterward. "We've heard back from Bepi — the spacecraft is now in contact with the ground and the teams at ESOC [the European Space Operations Centre] are busy assessing the telemetry. Flight Dynamics already has confirmed it achieved orbital capture around Mercury! Early next week we'll share the next update with the upcoming steps," the mission team said via X on Saturday evening. We've heard back from Bepi - the spacecraft is now in contact with the ground and the teams at ESOC are busy assessing the telemetry. item.title: SpaceX launches classified mission for US Space Force from California (video)
item.description: null SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force tonight (Nov. 20), sending a mystery payload to orbit from California's central coast. A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base tonight at 11:20 p.m. EST (8:20 p.m. local California time; 0420 GMT on Nov. 21), on a Space Force mission called USSF-317. The Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth about 8.5 minutes later, touching down in the Pacific Ocean atop the SpaceX drone ship "Of Course I Still Love You." It was the 11th launch and landing for this booster, which is designated B1100. A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launches the USSF-317 mission for the U.S. Space Force from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California on Nov. 20, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) SpaceX ended its launch webcast just after that touchdown, so we didn't get to see the Falcon 9's upper stage power its way to orbit. USSF-317 is a classified mission, so we don't know what the upper stage is carrying or where exactly it's headed. However, some experts think that USSF-317 may be hauling a batch of SpaceX's Starshield satellites to low Earth orbit (LEO) for the Space Force's Space Based Sensing and Targeting portfolio, which helps the military keep tabs on potential targets around the world. The Falcon 9's first stage rests on the deck of a drone ship after launching the USSF-317 mission. (Image credit: SpaceX) Previous Booster 1100 missions NROL-105 | USSF-385 | 8 Starlink missions USSF-317 was the 121st Falcon 9 launch of 2026 and the third mission that SpaceX has launched for the Space Force so far in November. The vast majority of this year's Falcon 9 missions — about 70% of them — have been devoted to building out SpaceX's Starlink LEO internet constellation, which currently consists of more than 11,000 satellites. The Falcon 9 has been putting up incredible numbers lately — it flew a whopping 165 times in 2025 , for example — but the workhorse rocket is on its way out . SpaceX plans to retire both it and the Falcon Heavy in favor of its fully reusable Starship megarocket, which deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites on its most recent two test flights .

item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 20, 1998: Russia launches 1st module of International Space Station as construction begins on the largest human-built structure in orbit
item.description: null On Nov. 20, 1998, the first piece of the International Space Station launched into orbit. The 42,000-pound module is called Zarya, and it's about the size of a tour bus. Zarya launched on board a Russian Proton rocket . Two weeks later, NASA's STS-88 shuttle mission aboard Endeavour brought the Unity module into space. The STS-88 astronauts connected the two modules in orbit. Zarya was built by the Russians, but it was paid for by the United States. NASA contracted a Russian company to build it for half the price of what the American company Lockheed Martin would have charged. These days, Zarya is mainly used for storage and for external fuel tanks. The module also has docking ports for Russian Progress cargo ships and Soyuz spacecraft that carry crews to and from the space station. Today, the I nternational Space Station is about the size of a football field and typically hosts up to seven crewmembers. But back in 1998, it was a pretty tight squeeze. A Russian Proton rocket launches the core Zarya module of the International Space Station (left), which can be seen in orbit (right) during the first mission to the station in 1998. (Image credit: NASA/Roscosmos) Why it mattered As of this writing, the International Space Station is 28 years old, and has seen steady rotating crews of astronauts since the year 2000 (for 26 years and counting). It is a marvel of space engineering, but every engineering marvel begins the same: with the first piece. And that is what the Zarya module is: The foundation of the International Space Station. Zarya, also known as the Functional Cargo Block (or Russian acronym FGB), is the core module of the space station around which every other module was attached. It weighed 42,600 pounds at launch and is just aver 41 feet long and 13.5 feet wide. Inside, it boasts a total habitable volume of 1,650 cubic feet. The Zarya and Unity modules are connecting in orbit to build the International Space Station. NASA The Zarya and Unity modules are connecting in orbit to build the International Space Station. NASA The Zarya and Unity modules are connecting in orbit to build the International Space Station. NASA NASA paid $220 million for Zarya's construction at the Krunichev State Research and Production Space Center in Moscow, with work beginning in 1994 and ending in 1998. The module is a central hub based on the success of Russia's Salyut space station designs , with two solar arrays for power and 16 external tanks to store propellant. While NASA's space shuttle Endeavour was the first to meet Zarya (and attach NASA's core Unity connecting module to it), it wasn't until Russia'z Zvezda service launched in 2000 and docked with Zarya's aft that the fledgling space station was large enough to accomodate its first three-person crew, Expedition 1. Over the last 28 years, giant backbone-like metal trusses, solar wings and many other modules (built by Russia, NASA, Europe, Canada and Japan) have greatly expanded the living area of t

item.title: Don't turn the moon into the Wild West, scientists warn
item.description:
Tereza is a London-based science and technology journalist, aspiring fiction writer and amateur gymnast. Originally from Prague, the Czech Republic, she spent the first seven years of her career working as a reporter, script-writer and presenter for various TV programmes of the Czech Public Service Television. She later took a career break to pursue further education and added a Master's in Science from the International Space University, France, to her Bachelor's in Journalism and Master's in Cultural Anthropology from Prague's Charles University. She worked as a reporter at the Engineering and Technology magazine, freelanced for a range of publications including Live Science, Space.com, Professional Engineering, Via Satellite and Space News and served as a maternity cover science editor at the European Space Agency.

Researchers are calling for a moratorium on industrial exploitation of the moon, fearing that rapid development could cause irreversible environmental damage and destroy invaluable scientific material. Both China and the U.S. are pushing forward with plans to establish permanent human settlements on the moon by the end of the next decade. Commercial players want to build businesses supporting these future explorers by mining for resources such as water , construction materials, industrial metals and rare earth minerals. However, some scientists argue that a temporary ban on lunar industrialization is necessary to allow regulations to catch up and limit what can be allowed in order to prevent a moon rush from destroying the pristine lunar environment. Two such researchers are Florian Rabitz, a professor of climate and technology governance at Vilnius University in Lithuania, and Xiao-Shan Yap, an assistant professor of Earth-space sustainability at Utrecht University in the Netherlands. In a piece published last month in the journal Global Environmental Politics , the pair call for "robust international regulations" and "broad and inclusive deliberation" to allow the global community to carefully consider the impact of economic activities on the moon. In addition to the threat to the scientifically priceless lunar landscape, the researchers also object to the colonization of the moon by a small number of powerful players — namely China, the U.S. and their respective close allies. "With the moon it's absolutely clear that whoever is doing the big infrastructure work is going to be asserting their position, including by defining their own exclusive territories," Rabitz said in a statement . "That shouldn't be the Wild West." Rabitz pointed out that, although the United Nations' 1967 Outer Space Treaty prevents individual nations from appropriating the moon, Earth's natural satellite and its valuable resources are unlikely to remain truly neutral territory if its exploitation is going to be led by a small number of powerful nations.

item.title: GTA hasn't gone to space (yet), but these sci-fi games can offer you a life of crime among the stars
item.description: GTA 6 has only just come out, and it's already taken the world by storm and positioned itself as one of the greatest games of all time . Great news for gamers, but what about sci-fi fans? To this day, Rockstar Games sadly hasn't embraced sci-fi with any of its open-world games (save for those UFO Easter eggs). It doesn't seem likely they'll journey to the stars anytime soon — you can't really do cutting societal satire about space — but that doesn't mean there aren't GTA-adjacent sci-fi adventures set in outer space. The frustrating thing is that no one has exactly cracked that pitch yet. Non-linear games set in outer space tend to be either too ambitious, like No Man's Sky, or too focused on specific experiences like space combat, like Star Wars: Squadrons. The end result is a roster of great sandboxes that let us journey to different star systems, but no game that dares to explore a criminal fantasy with the level of depth and opportunities seen in the last few Rockstar games. With new hardware powering far more complex open-world games, it's only a matter of time before "GTA in space" is a real thing. For now, there are some space games that let us explore sci-fi worlds, roleplaying as criminals and outlaws amongst the stars. Roleplaying a space outlaw (Image credit: Bethesda Softworks) Massive space RPGs like Starfield and The Outer Worlds 2 offer vast playgrounds you can explore and redefine through your actions. The lawful path is the obvious choice if you'd like to save the galaxy, but a life of crime awaits those who tire of the heroics. Starfield even has a "new game plus" mechanic baked into the player's journey, encouraging experimentation and living different lives, so if you stick with the divisive space RPG, the criminal life is all but unavoidable. And in traditional Bethesda fashion, you're not rushed to the next "main" objective, so if you want to become the most dangerous space criminal in the Settled Systems, you'll be supported by the mechanics and systems. You can always get back to saving the galaxy when you feel like it. (Image credit: Xbox Game Studios) The Outer Worlds 2 is another option if you want to become a star-surfing scoundrel. It might not be as absurdly expansive as Starfield, but Obsidian's whole deal has always been freedom of choice and roleplaying, so you can bet this humorous sequel also lets the protagonist become a bit of an a-hole. The main story already sets you in a collision course with corporate interests, too. Like in Mass Effect and other classic space RPGs, it's your choice to be either a goody-two-shoes or an edgy maniac, and I won't lie: the second option is usually more entertaining. Last but not least, there's a third game that also has enough going on to support a GTA-inspired fantasy in outer space: No Man's Sky . It's grown so much over the years that its original space exploration premise has been buried by content like fully customizable space stations, actual cities and towns

item.title: Trouble at Mars: NASA's Perseverance rover, Odyssey orbiter halt science work due to glitches
item.description: null Two of NASA's Mars explorers are sidelined by glitches at the moment. The Perseverance rover and Mars Odyssey orbiter have stood down from science work due to technical problems, NASA announced on Thursday (Nov. 19). Perseverance has been sidelined by an antenna issue, and the venerable Odyssey is dealing with a balky reaction wheel. NASA hopes both can get back to work at Mars by the end of November. Communication issues for Perseverance Perseverance landed inside Mars' Jezero Crater in February 2021, tasked with assessing the area's potential to support past life and with collecting dozens of samples for future return to Earth. It has done all this and more. The Perseverance team has determined that Jezero hosted a potentially habitable lake billions of years ago. And the car-sized rover has found a wealth of complex organic compounds in Martian rock, some of which might themselves be signs of life (though assessing this hypothesis fully will likely require bringing Perseverance's samples to Earth for analysis, scientists stress). In addition, Perseverance just set a new distance record for off-Earth driving, rolling past the mark set by its smaller cousin, NASA's Opportunity rover (28.06 miles, or 45.16 kilometers). Perseverance broke that record on Oct. 11. Just 19 days later, however, the mission team noticed a problem: The rover's main UHF downlink radio — which it uses to send information home to Earth, via data-relay satellites in Mars orbit — failed to send its usual "heartbeat" pings to the main computer. Perseverance detected this problem autonomously and reacted as it was programmed to do: The six-wheeled robot switched to its backup UHF radio and went into a protective "safe mode," shutting down all non-essential systems. The rover team recovered Perseverance from safe mode but soon noticed another issue: "The backup UHF radio was transmitting at about half of its expected power output," NASA officials wrote in an update on Thursday . Perseverance's handlers have stopped using that backup radio as well; the rover is now communicating with Earth directly (without the help of relay orbiters), sending signals to NASA's Deep Space Network dishes via its high-gain antenna. This pathway features lower data rates, and the mission team wants to prioritize the delivery of diagnostic information. So they've paused Perseverance's science work, which includes observations by its various cameras. The glitch may be disappointing to devoted Perseverance fans, many of whom have already noticed that the mission website hasn't uploaded any new raw images since Nov. 7 . But there's no reason to panic, according to NASA. "The rover is stable and communicating with the team," agency officials wrote in Thursday's update. "The team is hopeful the rover could return to science by the end of November, and NASA will provide further updates in the future as the team works the issue." Artist's illustration of NASA's Mars Odyssey orbiter circling the Red Pl

item.title: There's an impostor hiding in the Hyades star cluster. Can you spot it?
item.description: null For years I looked at Taurus and saw something perfectly sensible. There was the Hyades, the big V-shaped cluster that forms the bull's face, with Aldebaran, noticeably brighter and more orange than the other stars, the dominant star. Every diagram reinforced the arrangement — Aldebaran was the eye of Taurus, the Hyades made the face, and in my head they became one object. Then I discovered that Aldebaran has nothing to do with the Hyades. I remember going outside afterward and looking again, half expecting the deception to become obvious now that I knew. It didn't. Aldebaran still looked completely at home among the other stars . The difference is hidden in the one dimension our eyes judge poorly when we look into space — depth. Aldebaran is about 65 light-years away, while the Hyades are roughly 150 light-years distant. The orange eye of Taurus is a foreground star that happens to lie almost exactly along our line of sight toward the Hyades. This fact exposes one of the most convincing tricks in stargazing. The night sky looks flat, and our brains are extremely willing to believe it. But it has incredible depth — and when you can see parts of the night sky in 3D, that's when you begin to appreciate that you're not looking at a flat map. Instead, you begin to see our cosmic neighborhood as it really is. By appreciating depth, you learn its geography. What's happening and when to look Aldebaran, the brightest star in the constellation of Taurus. (Image credit: Christophe Lehenaff via Getty Images) Taurus is now easy to find from the Northern Hemisphere during the evening. Once it's dark, look east for a small, tight knot of stars — the Pleiades open cluster (M45) — and then look nearby for a much larger V-shaped arrangement. That V is the Hyades, with unmistakably orange Aldebaran apparently sitting on one arm. Aldebaran's name is derived from the Arabic Al Dabarān, meaning "the follower," because it appears to trail the Pleiades across the night sky. The Hyades is a real physical group of stars — an open cluster — that formed together and moves through our galaxy together. About 153 light-years away, the Hyades is the nearest open star cluster to Earth. The name means "the rainmakers" because their rising and setting times in the ancient Greek sky coincided with wet weather. The stars in the Hyades are of a similar age — and mostly sun-like stars, or similar — so astronomers can tell that they all formed together in the same nebula . Orange-red star Aldebaran — the 14th-brightest star in the night sky — is the interloper, sitting less than half as far away from the sun . If you could somehow view the neighborhood from another part of the Milky Way , the familiar arrangement would fall apart. Aldebaran would no longer sit conveniently in the bull's face, and Taurus itself would stop looking like a bull. Constellations aren't objects in the same sense as a planet or star cluster. They are merely views. Even stars that appear almost side by si

item.title: Could an ancient solar eclipse rewrite Egyptian history?
item.description: null The solar system is a clock that can be run in both directions. On Aug. 2, 2027, that clock will bring the moon's dark central shadow — a path of totality — back to Egypt. A t otal solar eclipse will sweep across the country , passing directly over Luxor and plunging some of ancient Egypt's greatest surviving monuments into darkness. Totality will begin in Luxor at approximately 1:02 p.m. EEST and last 6 minutes 22 seconds, according to Time and Date . We know when it will happen because we can calculate the motions of Earth and the moon centuries in advance. But run the same celestial clock backward and eclipses become one of nature's most precise timestamps. Astronomers can reconstruct where the moon's shadow fell thousands of years ago, even when nobody left a record of it. When an ancient text reliably describes an eclipse, it can anchor a moment in history to a specific place and time. Did an eclipse rewrite the Pyramid Age? Pharaoh Shepseskaf's huge rectangular tomb at South Saqqara (Image credit: Jon Bodsworth - www.egyptarchive.co.uk) We know from astronomical calculations that eclipses crossed Egypt long before anyone left an identifiable written record of one. On April 1, 2471 B.C., a total solar eclipse swept across northern Egypt during the age of the great pyramid builders. In research published in 2025, archaeoastronomer Giulio Magli at the Polytechnic University of Milan proposed that the eclipse may help explain why Pharaoh Shepseskaf broke with tradition and built a huge rectangular tomb at South Saqqara instead of a pyramid. It's a tantalizing hypothesis, but no surviving Egyptian text records the eclipse. Astronomers can calculate that an eclipse happened, but using it as a historical timestamp requires evidence that someone actually saw it and recorded it. That's where an eclipse almost 1,300 years later becomes particularly intriguing. Is the oldest recorded eclipse hidden in the Bible? Researchers have proposed that an annular eclipse occurred over Canaan on Oct. 30, 1207 BC, and may be described in the Bible. This image was captured during an annular solar eclipse from Redding, California on May 20, 2012. (Image credit: Paul Souders via Getty Images) A passage in the Old Testament book of Joshua describes the sun and moon as if they stopped in the sky. After leading the people of Israel into Canaan — modern-day Israel and Palestine — Joshua prayed: "Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and moon, in the Valley of Aijalon. And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped, until the nation took vengeance on their enemies." Ancient Gibeon is about six miles (10 kilometers) northwest of Jerusalem. In research published in 2017, researchers Colin Humphreys and Graeme Waddington at Cambridge University in the U.K. claimed it could refer to an annular solar eclipse on Oct. 30, 1207 B.C. It's a controversial interpretation, not least because it depends on exactly how the ancient Hebrew text is translated. However, if correct, it could be t

item.title: Russia is developing a nuclear space weapon, US intelligence report finds
item.description: null Last month, the U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) released a chilling and info-packed report judging the scope and breadth of threats posed by the nation's adversaries in space. The new report focuses on China , Russia and the emerging space powers of Iran and North Korea. It looks at what's happening in Earth orbit and beyond, including cislunar space, the region between our planet and the moon . The report — the 2026 edition of "Challenges to Security in Space" — is the third iteration of the DIA's unclassified intelligence assessment on space-related challenges and threats to U.S. national security, as well as the extent to which space is treated internationally as a warfighting domain . Information within the report, which you can read here , is current as of July 2026. DIA's mission is to provide intelligence on foreign militaries to help prevent wars, and win the ones that are fought. Up-front finding The report's up-front finding is that China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea are developing, testing, deploying and using space capabilities "in a way that threatens the security of all space systems and their associated space benefits." Indeed, China and Russia are developing "a formidable spectrum" of offensive capabilities to degrade or destroy space services of other countries, from kinetic destruction to sophisticated jamming and cyber operations. The DIA report also notes that "the production of cheaper, smaller, and simpler satellites , which are faster to develop and deploy, along with the expansion of commercially available launch services, are driving the rapid integration of commercial space alternatives to support national security." While space commercialization is making previously government-centered space services widely available to interested parties, the DIA report adds, that availability also includes state and non-state actors with malign interests. There are a range of threats to space-based services, both commercial and military. Some are reversible, while others are not. (Image credit: DIA) Counterspace worries A major item dealt with by the DIA is "counterspace" — and it's not the kind that you'll find in your kitchen. Counterspace operations can be either offensive or defensive. They can be used on purpose to reversibly or irreversibly deny, disrupt, degrade, damage or destroy a space object or component of a space system. Here are the key elements of counterspace, as identified within the DIA report: Antisatellite (ASAT) missiles are designed to kinetically strike and destroy satellites. ASAT missiles could produce massive amounts of debris that can remain in orbit for decades or even centuries. Physical or cyberattacks against ground sites and other terrestrial infrastructure supporting space operations can also threaten satellite services. item.title: Asali Africa: Serves Up ‘There’s Rice at Home’ A New Cooking Series Hosted by Chef Soliat Bada
item.description: Chef Soliat Bada Anyone who grew up in a Nigerian home knows the line. You suggest buying food outside, and before you finish the sentence, someone reminds you that there’s rice at home. It is usually the end of the conversation. In Asali Africa’s new series, it is where the conversation starts. There’s Rice at Home is a cooking and conversation show from Asali Africa, the Lagos-based creative development agency, hosted by Chef Soliat Bada . In each episode, Soliat cooks one rice dish with a guest, and while the pot does its work, the two get into the kind of talk that usually happens around food: family, money and what success really looks like. Rice is the most ordinary thing in a Nigerian kitchen, and the show makes a good case that it doesn’t have to taste ordinary. Over five episodes, released every two weeks, the menu travels from Jamaica to Saudi Arabia, back home to Nigeria and on to Louisiana. You don’t just watch the food get made, either. The recipes are written up in full on Asali Africa’s website, with the ingredients and method laid out step by step, so you can watch Soliat cook a dish and then make it in your own kitchen. The season opens with Rice and Peas with Oxtail, the Jamaican Sunday staple of rice cooked in coconut milk with red kidney beans (the “peas”), served beside rich, slow-cooked oxtail. Soliat’s guest is Michael Famoroti , co-founder of Stears, and their conversation turns to family and black tax: the expectation that once you start earning, you start supporting the people who raised you. Read the full recipe for Rice and Peas with Oxtail . Rice and peas with oxtail, from Episode 1 Soliat Bada and Michael Famoroti in Episode 1 Episode 2 moves to the Gulf for lamb kabsa, Saudi Arabia’s national dish, fragrant with dried lime and seven spice. Soliat is joined by Bella Adeleke , CEO of Asali Africa and founder of the fashion label Garbe, for a conversation about redefining success. Read the full recipe for Lamb Kabsa . Lamb kabsa, from Episode 2 Still to come are Nigerian fried rice with fried turkey and dodo, cooked with Toyin Jolapamo and Nneoma Mere; jambalaya with Goldie Iyamu and Vanessa Iloenyosi ; and a season finale with Edwin Okolo and Temi Omolehinwa. For more on Asali Africa and the products and ideas it develops, visit asali.africa . Episodes 1 and 2 are out now on YouTube. Watch Episode 1 below. https://www.youtube.com/embed/-6Ux0-vNDnw Sponsored Content The post Asali Africa: Serves Up ‘There’s Rice at Home’ A New Cooking Series Hosted by Chef Soliat Bada appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. item.title: Beyond the Mini LED Label: What Should Define Good Mini LED Performance?
item.description: The presence of Mini LED tells a shopper something important about the light source behind an LCD panel. It does not, by itself, explain how that light is arranged, divided or controlled. Those implementation choices can have a major influence on contrast, black level performance, highlight control and the visibility of blooming in difficult scenes. From Presence To Performance That distinction matters because a category becomes more useful to consumers when it can be evaluated through clear performance principles rather than through a technology name alone. For Mini LED, three factors provide a practical starting point. The first is hardware local dimming. In a hardware based system, physical groups of LEDs can be brightened, dimmed or switched off independently across different areas of the screen. This gives the television more direct control over how light is distributed within a single image. The second is local dimming zone count and precision. A higher number of independently controlled zones can allow the backlight to respond in smaller areas, which can improve separation between bright highlights and surrounding dark regions when other major conditions are comparable. The number itself is not the whole story, but it is a useful indicator of how granular the backlight system can be. The third is backlight architecture. Full Array Local Dimming places controllable zones across the area behind the panel, providing the physical foundation for more localized light management than designs that illuminate the panel from the edges or operate the backlight more uniformly. Together, these three elements move the Mini LED conversation from a simple question of whether the technology is present to a more useful question: how effectively is the light being controlled? Where TCL Enters The Category Conversation TCL is relevant to that discussion because Mini LED has become a significant part of its global television business. According to Omdia data cited in TCL Electronics interim results, TCL ranked No. 1 globally by Mini LED TV shipment volume in the first half of 2026. TCL reported 2.43 million Mini LED TV shipments during the period, representing 77.1% year on year growth. That position follows a strong 2025, when TCL reported, based on Omdia data, a 31.1% share of global Mini LED TV shipments and 118.0% year on year shipment growth. Market scale does not, on its own, define technology leadership. What it does provide is evidence that a manufacturer has become an important participant in how the category develops. For a company operating at that scale, leadership increasingly includes helping make the technology easier to understand and giving consumers clearer ways to evaluate what they are buying. Defining Category Leadership Category leadership in Mini LED should therefore be broader than shipment rankings. item.title: How Columbus Crew turned it all around to set up MLS playoff showdown vs. Messi
item.description: It wasn’t working. Issa Tall had to admit that. Well, he didn’t really have to. The results told the story for him. The Columbus Crew didn’t win in its first five MLS matches. By the World Cup break, 15 games in, they’d only added two more. There needed to be changes, and they needed to be big. The Crew general manager moved quickly. In May, he fired coach Henrik Rydström, his first coaching hire as the Crew’s chief soccer officer, though he was quick to point out he was involved with previous hires including bringing in Wilfried Nancy. He spent big in the summer, revamping the Crew’s attack and adding pieces while bidding farewell to some regulars. Ten players arrived, and eight went out. It worked. The Crew turned the boat around, going from worst in the Eastern Conference to closing the season on a six-game win streak and having won eight of their last nine. That was enough not only to jump out of Thursday’s wild card match but to set up a First Round playoff series with Inter Miami, the reigning champion led by Lionel Messi. They also pushed to the U.S. Open Cup final, falling to St. Louis City in a penalty shootout. All of it led Tall to believe he made the right decisions, moving on quickly from the coach he thought was the right man for the job. “Some people could’ve waited the full year. Maybe it would’ve been safer, but that’s not me. That’s not us as a club. That’s not even the way we play!” Tall told USA TODAY Sports ahead of the playoffs. “You see how we are bold and are not afraid of taking risk. At the end of the day, it wasn’t even a risk necessarily. It was necessary for our players, for our club as a whole and I think ultimately we made the right decision to do it at that time.” Tall still stands by Rydström as a good coach, something he’s proving while leading Hammarby in Sweden which currently sits atop of the table after running off five consecutive wins. But he wasn’t the right fit for the Crew in the post-Nancy era. The Crew turned to Courtois, a former Crew academy and MLS Next Pro coach who continued the idea first expressed on the field so successfully by Nancy’s teams. The squad might not have been the entirely right squad, either. Tall turned to a scouting network led by Mark Nichols, bringing in a proven MLS veteran in Santi Rodriguez, Chile national team forward Gonzalo Tapia, securing a loan deal for Moroccan winger Anass Zaroury and signing designated player Brais Mendez, a Spanish attacker whose arrival from Real Sociedad brought to mind that of Cucho Hernandez. While Mendez is at a different stage of his carer than Hernandez was, he turned into a star in Columbus, showing his full potential in MLS after frustrating stints with Watford and loans in Huseca, Mallorca and Getafe. Those new players bolstered a core that had been depleted by player movement but still included veteran defender Steven Moreira, homegrown center back Sean Zawadzki, fullback Mo Farsi - formerly a futsal specialist who the current Crew staff

item.title: ISS astronauts look down on the snow-capped Himalayas | Space photo of the day for Nov. 20, 2026
item.description: null A snapshot of the Himalayas captured from aboard the ISS. (Image credit: CSA/Joshua Kutryk) The Himalayas tower below the clouds, capped in icy snow in new snapshots captured from aboard the International Space Station . What is it? Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk was looking out one of the windows aboard the space station when the most incredible view came into focus — and thankfully he had a camera handy and was able to capture these striking scenes of the Himalayas from space. Above the mountain range, fluffy clouds hang in the atmosphere. Below, the expansive Himalayas are covered in bright snow and ice, which looks somehow both white and blue at the same time as the bright sunlight streaks across the breathtaking expanse. This frosty winter scene showcases the mountain range from orbit, from about 250 miles (400 kilometers) above Earth's surface. But even from this distance, the magnitude of this mountain range is palpable. The Himalayas stretch across five different countries including Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan. And the Himalayas include some of the highest mountain peaks on planet Earth, including Mount Everest. Himalayas 🗻 https://t.co/IzGzu20H4Q November 17, 2026 Why is it incredible? From orbit around Earth, you might expect even the largest landmarks on our planet to appear miniscule. But somehow, in these photographs snapped by Kutryk during NASA's SpaceX Crew-13 mission , even from hundreds of miles above our planet you can really see and feel the immense scale of this mammoth mountain range. It's unclear exactly where above the mountain range these photographs were taken, but it is always amazing to think that within these sweeping landscapes are people living their lives, likely unaware that an astronaut is taking in the beauty of their home. Perhaps somewhere hidden under the clouds in one of Kutryk's photographs are hikers climbing up the side of Mt. Everest, completing their own bucket list adventure as the astronauts watching from above complete theirs.

item.title: Lagos Hosts 2026 International Theatre Festival, Featuring Local and International Productions
item.description: The third edition of the Lagos International Theatre Festival (LITF) has concluded successfully, attracting over 20,000 attendees from November 9 to 15, 2026. Featuring more than 25 productions, international performances from Kenya, Brazil, Norway and Canada, high-profile diplomatic engagements and a spectacular Opening Night Gala, the festival reinforced its growing position as an important platform for showcasing Nigerian creativity and connecting global theatre communities. The impressive turnout, diversity of productions and international participation demonstrated the growing appetite for live theatre and the potential of cultural platforms to stimulate creative enterprise, encourage international collaboration and strengthen Nigeria’s global cultural presence. A Vision For Global Recognition Speaking on the success of the festival, Founder and Creative Producer, Bolanle Austen-Peters , said: “Our ambition has always been to create more than a theatre festival. We want to build a platform that places Lagos firmly on the global cultural map, gives African stories the international visibility they deserve and creates meaningful opportunities for our artists. Welcoming over 20,000 attendees, presenting more than 25 productions and bringing international performers from four countries to Lagos is a powerful affirmation of this vision. Theatre is not just entertainment; it is an instrument of cultural identity, economic opportunity and global influence. The Stage Is Everywhere, and Africa must claim its rightful place on that stage.” A Week Of Culture And Collaboration The festival opened on November 9 with Theatre Meets Food at Kaly Restaurant, featuring celebrated chef Hilda Baci in a unique fusion of culinary artistry and live performance. The week also featured diplomatic and cultural engagements hosted by the United States Consul General in Lagos and the British Embassy, alongside a networking reception organised by the British Council for festival directors and participating production companies. These engagements highlighted the importance of international partnerships and cultural diplomacy in advancing Nigeria’s creative industry. A Celebration Of Excellence A major highlight was the Opening Night Gala, held on November 13 at Shell Hall, MUSON Centre, which welcomed over 1,000 guests, including the Governor of Lagos State, Babajide Olusola Sanwo-Olu ; the Chargé d’Affaires of the US Mission in Nigeria; the US Consul General; the British Deputy High Commissioner; the Consul General of Brazil; the Consul General of South Africa, the Ambassador of the Republic of Korea; alongside other members of the diplomatic corps, heads of institutions, government representatives, international delegates and leading figures in the creative industry. item.title: I got to tour SpaceX's Starfactory facility in Starbase, Texas, and what I saw blew my mind
item.description: null STARBASE, Texas — I just finished covering the Starship Flight 15 mission, and SpaceXs incredible launch tower catch of the returned Ship 42 spacecraft isn't the only thing over the weekend that left me speechless. The morning of the launch (Nov. 13), SpaceX invited media on a tour of Starbase's Starfactory facility, where it manufactures and assembles both stages of its massive Starship rocket - an unprecedented behind-the-scenes look at the production and scale of SpaceX's operations, and a glimpse of things to come as Starship notches more and more milestones the more it flies. For some context, the five-story-tall Starfactory spans approximately 1 million square feet (~93,000 meters), with operations split between Starship's Super Heavy boosters and upper stage Ships, and nearly 330,000 additional square feet (30,000 square meters) of office space. SpaceX officials describe its design as one more akin to an automotive manufacturing plant than that of a typical aerospace production site, and inside, it is absolutely alive with activity. Inside Starfactory We entered through an arch-covered doorway underneath the giant "X" sign on the building's shorter face. Our media gaggle was met with curious glances as we were shown through the doors and guided onto the factory floor - few are ever able to cross that threshold outside of SpaceX employees, and our presence seemed as novel to those busy working as it was to us. Inside, we were struck with the sheer enormity of Starship's scale. Giant stainless-steel rocket parts were meticulously scattered across different subassembly stations throughout the building, with Ship nose cones, cylindrical sections and booster components all under various stages of manufacture. The sheer quantity of the hardware was staggering, and being so close to each as we walked Starfactory's throughways was an eye-opener. The exterior of SpaceX's Starfactory facility at Starbase, Texas. (Image credit: Josh Dinner/Future) Starbase is a unique partnership of privately-owned SpaceX property and publicly-accessible land and shoreline, which has created the unique ability for anyone with a mind to do so to drive right up to the the Starship launch pad to see the facilities up close (within a few hundred feet or so, which, as rockets go, is very, very close). Fully stacked, Starship stands more than 400 feet (120 meters) tall. Standing next to such a towering colossus on the pad is enough to drive home just how big the launch vehicle is, but standing next its segmented components inside Starfactory is even more humbling; like seeing one of Ship's upper aerodynamic flaps, which are each large enough when laid flat that you could park a pair of large SUVs on their faces with room to spare. item.title: Einstein was right! Scientists verify 1st image of a black hole ever captured
item.description: null An independent team of researchers has validated the first image of a supermassive black hole captured by humanity. That, in turn, verifies Einstein's greatest theory, general relativity , which first predicted the existence of black holes and what their immediate surroundings would look like. Captured by a global network of telescopes forming an interferometer called the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) and revealed to the public in 2019, the image shows the supermassive black hole at the heart of the galaxy Messier 87 (M87), located 55 million light-years away. The image of this black hole , designated M87*, with a mass around 6.5 billion times that of the sun, was an immense scientific achievement. That may lead to the question: why did it need verifying at all? Team leader and researcher with Australia's Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO), Samuel Lai explained why capturing the image of a distant black hole is so tricky. "It is like standing in your backyard and trying to take a photo of a doughnut on the moon," Lai said in a statement sent to Space.com via email. Lai and his small Australian team developed advanced machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques to capture information about the black hole's structure and filter out interference resulting from the fact that the EHT was viewing M87* from within our planet's atmosphere. The machine-learning technique called GenDIReCT also accounted for biases introduced by combining telescopes to create an Earth-sized interferometer. "When we applied it to the original EHT dataset, we found a black hole almost identical in size and shape as the historic EHT image. Importantly, our model had no idea what a black hole looked like when we applied it to the M87 data," Lai continued. "This is the first truly independent validation of the EHT image, an important step in the scientific process." This could settle the questions of just how the final image of M87* was influenced by both atmospheric effects and the processing methods needed to reconstruct pictures from telescope data. That's not just good news for the EHT; it's good news for Einstein. Take it away Einstein Einstein published his theory of general relativity in 1915, completely reshaping how we think of gravity. General relativity suggested that objects with mass curve the very fabric of space and time, united as a single entity called spacetime. Gravity arises from that curvature. The greater the mass, the more extreme the curvature and thus the greater the gravitational influence of that object. Taking this to its extreme, scientist Karl Schwarzschild came up with a solution to the equations of general relativity that suggested an infinitesimal region with infinite mass, resulting in unrestrained curvature, a singularity. Around this would be a spherical boundary at which not even light has the velocity needed to escape this region. Referred to as the Schwarzschild radius, that boundary became

item.title: SpaceX Dragon cargo capsule returns to Earth from the ISS
item.description: null SpaceX's 35th Dragon cargo mission has come home to Earth. The robotic Dragon capsule undocked from the International Space Station (ISS) on Friday (Nov. 20) at 12:05 p.m. EST (1705 GMT), while the duo were flying 260 miles (418 kilometers) above western China. The freighter made its way Earthward over the next 29 hours, ultimately splashing down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of California on Saturday (Nov. 21) at 5:03 p.m. EST (2155 GMT). The Dragon launched Oct. 13, on a mission called CRS-35 because it was the 35th that SpaceX has flown for NASA's Commercial Resupply Services program. The capsule arrived at the ISS on Oct. 15 , delivering more than 6,300 pounds (2,860 kilograms) of food, scientific gear and other supplies to the astronauts aboard the orbiting lab. It brought a lot of stuff down to Earth, too. "Thousands of pounds of cargo are returning from the space station, including research samples that could advance future space exploration and improve life on Earth," NASA officials wrote in an update on Tuesday (Nov. 17). "The returning research includes a 3D-bioprinted blood vessel construct scientists used to study vascular aging and cardiovascular disease in space and on Earth ," they added. Dragon is the only cargo craft flying today that's capable of making such downward deliveries. The others — Northrop Grumman's Cygnus, Russia's Progress vehicle and Japan's HTV-X — are all expendable and burn up in Earth's atmosphere to wrap up their first and only spaceflight. Editor's note: This story was updated at 12:20 p.m. ET on Nov. 20 with news of successful undocking, then again at 8:55 p.m. ET on Nov. 21 with news of splashdown.

item.title: Voyager 1 team, unbowed by communications glitch, celebrates epic 1-light-day distance milestone
item.description: null PASADENA, Calif. – NASA's Voyager mission team cheered and wiped away tears here on Thursday (Nov. 19), celebrating a big milestone — Voyager 1 just reached one light-day from Earth , something no other spacecraft has ever done. The excitement persisted despite a communication anomaly that cropped up on the probe, which the team remains confident is temporary. Voyager team members gathered for a press conference about the mission at the Von Karman auditorium here at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) — the first such Voyager event since 1989, when Voyager 1's twin, Voyager 2 , flew past Neptune. The gathering served to celebrate Voyager 1 's distance milestone: At 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT) on Wednesday (Nov. 18), the probe reached one light-day from Earth — the distance a photon travels in one day, which is about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers). That means it now takes a full day for a signal to travel from Earth to Voyager 1, the farthest human-made object out in space. "I remember in 1977 I was standing at the Cape watching Voyager launch, and I never thought I would be here today, 49 years later, to celebrate Voyager's one light-day. What an incredible milestone," Voyager project scientist Linda Spilker said during Thursday's event. An unexpected, but manageable, anomaly While this day and this week have been chock-full of excitement over the distance milestone, the Voyager mission team has been hard at work, as usual, keeping the two nearly 50-year-old spacecraft alive and functioning. Unfortunately, as JPL spokesperson Raquel Villanueva shared at this celebration, on Saturday (Nov. 14), Voyager 1 stopped transmitting science and engineering data. The team has remained in contact with Voyager 1 while investigating the issue, and they are confident that they'll be able to solve it soon. NASA and Voyager team members celebrate Voyager 1's light-day milestone at NASA JPL on Nov. 19, 2026. From left to right: Nicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate; Jonathan Lunine, chief scientist, NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory; Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager; Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager; Jamie Rankin, Voyager deputy project scientist. (Image credit: Chelsea Gohd) "We listen to each spacecraft every day," Voyager project manager Suzanne Dodd told Space.com at the event. Regarding Voyager 1, "we have an anomaly that is not something unseen before," Dodd said. "We do have a very strong carrier signal. We currently don't have a frame sync, so we're not getting the science or engineering data currently." "But if you recall," Dodd added, "one light-day is very far from us. [It takes] 24 hours to get the signal to the spacecraft, 24 hours for the signal to come down, so it takes two days to diagnose anything on the spacecraft … So we can't do anything fast, and the data rates are very low." According to Dodd, this anomaly isn't a major cause for long-term concern. Rather, it's likely just part of the na

item.title: On this day in space! Nov. 19, 2005: Japan's Hayabusa spacecraft makes 1st-ever liftoff from surface of an asteroid
item.description: null On Nov. 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft made the first liftoff from an asteroid. Hayabusa was supposed to return asteroid samples to Earth. Asteroids are space rocks that were formed during the early solar system. We study asteroids to learn more about the solar system's history. Hayabusa (pronounced HI-uh-BOOS-uh) made two touchdowns on asteroid Itokawa (EE -toh-KA-wah). Each time, the spacecraft went into safe mode. Controllers weren't sure if Hayabusa gathered any material. But they sent the spacecraft back to Earth anyway. Hayabusa's sample return capsule returned to Earth in June 2010 . Scientists found dust of Itokawa inside the capsule, proving that it did indeed capture samples of Itokawa. An artist's illustration of Japan's Hayabusa spacecraft landing on asteroid Itokawa. (Image credit: JAXA) Why it mattered The primary goal of Japan's Hayabusa mission to asteroid Itokawa was never to be the first spacecraft to liftoff from a space rock. The mission was always aimed at collecting samples from an asteroid and returning them to Earth. It was a hard road to Itokawa for Hayabusa. The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) launched the probe on May 9, 2003, with plans for an arrival at the asteroid in the early summer of 2005. That asteroid arrival was delayed until September 2005 after a solar storm degraded Hayabusa's solar arrays, limiting the available power for its ion engines. The asteroid Itokawa as seen by Japan's Hayabusa spacecraft. (Image credit: JAXA) Still, Hayabusa managed to limp along its path to reach the asteroid Itokawa on Sept. 12, 2005. Hayabusa dropped a small lander onto Itokawa, but that probe was apparently lost. Hayabusa then dropped a landing target on the asteroid, and ultimately managed to touchdown about 99 feet from the marker, JAXA has said. During its first landing on Nov. 19, Hayabusa descended to a point just 56 feet above Itokawa before going silent for 3 hours, according to an Associated Press report . Once contact was restored, JAXA officials confirmed the probe had landed, and it eventually lifted off for a second attempt. That was the first-ever liftoff from an asteroid by a spacecraft. "The spacecraft actually bounced off the surface a few times and spent about 39 minutes resting on the asteroid, but apparently the samplers never fired," Andrew Cheng, a Hayabusa science team member at Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory, told Space.com at the time . There was hope that some material managed to make it inside the collector anyway. "After all the thrashing about ... there is no way to confirm that," Cheng had said. The second landing on Itokawa occured a few days later on Nov. 26, 2005. In November 2010, five months after Hayabusa's sample-return capsule touched down in Australia, JAXA announced some good news: Hayabusa did collect 1,500 dust grains from asteroid Itokawa, samples that were jammed into the collector by the two landings, despite is collector mechanism not

item.title: The view from the tower: Watch Starship come in for chopsticks catch in epic slo-mo video
item.description: null A new set of slo-mo videos gives us a new perspective on SpaceX's first-ever recovery of a Starship upper stage. The company notched the milestone on Saturday (Nov. 14), when the launch tower at its Starbase site in South Texas caught Starship's Ship spacecraft with its "chopstick" arms. You've probably seen photos and videos showing the epic snag from afar. But on Tuesday (Nov. 17), SpaceX released up-close views — a series of four slo-mo videos captured by cameras near the top of the 480-foot-tall (146 meters) tower. The Ship upper stage of SpaceX's Starship megarocket comes back to its launch tower for a "chopsticks" catch on Nov. 14, 2026, during the vehicle's 15th test flight. (Image credit: SpaceX) "The Starbase tower chopsticks catching their first Starship. This unique architecture was designed for full and rapid reusability, enabling repeat launches and landings from the same pad," SpaceX wrote in a Tuesday X post that shared the videos, a compilation of which you can see embedded above. Starship is the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built. Its current "V3" version stands about 408 feet (124 m) tall, and future iterations will be even larger . As SpaceX noted in Tuesday's post, the megarocket is also designed to be fully and rapidly reusable — a first for an orbital launch system. The company plans to catch both Starship stages — Ship and the Super Heavy booster — at the launch tower, a recovery strategy designed to enable efficient inspection, refurbishment and reflight. Another view of the chopsticks catch on Nov. 14. (Image credit: SpaceX) SpaceX planned to carry out such a double catch on this most recent test flight , Starship's 15th to date, which launched on Friday evening (Nov. 13). But Super Heavy experienced a low-fuel warning during its return to Starbase about 6.5 minutes after launch and autonomously diverted to splash down in the Gulf of Mexico. That wasn't a huge deal for SpaceX, as it had already caught Super Heavy on three previous test flights . Snagging Ship is tougher; the upper stage returns to Earth from orbit, so it comes in faster and hotter than the booster does. SpaceX had not even attempted a Ship catch before Flight 15. But the company managed to pull off the maneuver on its first try. And Ship did some work in orbit before coming home: It deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 broadband satellites on Flight 15, the second batch that the company has sent to low Earth orbit . The first set was deployed on Flight 14 , which launched on Sept. 28.

item.title: A Safari, a Beach & Easy Entry? 5 African Spots for Your Christmas Holiday
item.description: Five African destinations Nigerian passport holders can visit visa-free or with visa on arrival this Christmas holiday. Image: AI-generated. The group chat has the concerts, the dinners and the Detty December link-ups covered. But has anyone planned the getaway? Beyond the usual Lagos parties and end-of-year outings, there is a whole continent waiting to be explored, with sun-soaked beaches, wildlife safaris, exciting food scenes and cities with plenty of stories to tell. You do not have to spend weeks navigating embassy appointments and visa applications to make it happen, either. Several African countries offer Nigerian passport holders visa-free entry or visas on arrival, making a festive-season escape much easier to plan. Whether you are travelling solo, gathering your friends, taking the family along or joining a curated travel group, here are five destinations worth considering for your Christmas holiday. Kenya Imagine spotting lions and giraffes against a city skyline before breakfast, then catching an evening flight or train straight to the coast for fresh seafood by the Indian Ocean. That contrast is what makes Kenya such a rewarding December escape. Nairobi gives you immediate access to wildlife at Nairobi National Park and the Giraffe Centre alongside lively restaurants and art spaces in Westlands and Karen, while longer itineraries open up classic game drives in the Maasai Mara, views of Mount Kilimanjaro in Amboseli, and warm beach days in Diani or Watamu. Nigerian citizens enjoy visa-free entry for short stays of up to 60 days without needing a paid eTA, leaving more room in your budget for safaris and coastal stays. Rwanda Not everyone wants their year-end holiday to feel like a non-stop sprint, and Rwanda is built for travellers who prefer scenery, clean air, and an unhurried pace. Days in Kigali easily revolve around specialty coffee shops, contemporary art at Inema Arts Center, and a sobering, essential visit to the Kigali Genocide Memorial before you head out into the countryside. From the capital, you can track chimpanzees and walk above the trees in Nyungwe Forest, go on wildlife drives in Akagera National Park, or spend quiet afternoons along the shores of Lake Kivu. With 30-day visa-free entry for Nigerian passport holders, getting there is straightforward from start to finish. Mauritius Sometimes a proper Christmas break calls for leaving mainland schedules behind altogether for turquoise lagoons, catamaran cruises, and mountain trails. In Mauritius, you can base yourself around Grand Baie in the north for boat trips to Île aux Cerfs and lively beachside dinners, or head south-west toward Le Morne Brabant for coastal hikes and water sports. Between beach days, the bustling Central Market in Port Louis, the lush trails of Black River Gorges National Park, and Casela Nature Parks keep a week-long itinerary full without ever feeling hectic. item.title: Esther Adeyanju: This International Men’s Day, Let’s Make Room for Men’s Vulnerability
item.description: “Men are not wired to show emotions.” A male friend once said to me during an argument. He was so convinced that I wondered whether a manual somewhere explained how men were manufactured. According to him, men were created to be strong, endure pain and keep their emotions to themselves. That was simply how they were made. “So, because you’re a man, you’re not supposed to feel hurt, fear or disappointment?” I disagreed. He insisted that showing emotions was not in a man’s nature. Who made that rule? Who decided that men could experience pain but must never be seen expressing it? At what point did being a man become synonymous with pretending that everything was fine? The conversation wilted, but it has stayed with me, perhaps because my friend wasn’t expressing an unusual opinion. He was repeating a stereotype many of us have heard all our lives: “Boys don’t cry.” “Be a man.” “Man up.” Three little expressions, and somewhere between being told to be strong and learning to say “I’m fine,” I wonder how many men have forgotten what it feels like to be heard. Frequent questions men are asked: “How far? Work nko?” “When are you getting married?” “Have you bought land?” “How is the family?” And the famous Nigerian question that can make an unemployed graduate dread family gatherings: “So, what are you doing now?” We often inquire about their achievements, responsibilities, and plans. These aspects are important, but how often do we ask about their fears? A father who leaves home before sunrise and returns exhausted, burdened by the weight of school fees, rent, and family expectations. A young graduate who has submitted countless job applications, yet still smiles politely when another relative inquires why he hasn’t found a job. A successful professional whose LinkedIn profile showcases numerous achievements, while his personal life tells a story that no one has thought to ask about. We admire their strength, we applaud their sacrifices, and we celebrate their accomplishments. But what about what they are going through? The person everyone leans on also needs somewhere to lean. Society has an interesting checklist for measuring a man’s success. A good job, a house, a car, a wife, children and financial stability. Preferably, all achieved before a certain age. But if a man struggles to achieve all these, is his life any less meaningful? Surely, a man’s worth cannot be reduced to his bank balance, job title or ability to convince everyone that he has everything under control. There must be room for men who are still becoming. The Empty Chair Nobody Notices This year’s theme for International Men’s Day, celebrated on November 19th, is “The Future Is Everyone.” While this theme may seem straightforward, it invites us to explore the true meaning of “everyone.” Working in corporate communications at the Chartered Institute of Personnel Management of Nigeria (CIPM) has heightened my awareness of how easily we categorise people based on their roles: leaders, em

item.title: How La Roche-Posay Brought Skin Science to Over 500 Guests in Its First Living Lab Experience
item.description: La Roche-Posay concluded its first Living Lab experience in Nigeria, welcoming Nigerian stakeholders to its opening party and three-day programme, held from 4 to 6 November 2026 at Oasis by The Five Palm, Victoria Island, Lagos. Inspired by the original Living Lab concept in Paris, the experience brought the science, research and expertise behind skincare closer to Nigerian consumers and healthcare professionals. It marked the brand’s first Living Lab in the country, creating a platform for more accessible conversations around skin health, dermatological innovation and everyday skincare. The experience opened with an exclusive session for healthcare professionals and invited guests before welcoming members of the public over the following two days. Each day featured three expert-led sessions exploring the role of dermatology and scientific research in advancing skin health, the wider impact of skin conditions on everyday life, and the importance of understanding product safety, tolerance and efficacy. The sessions brought together healthcare professionals and representatives from across Nigeria’s dermatological beauty and skincare community, encouraging knowledge-sharing and stronger connections between science, expertise and consumer education. Visitors explored five dedicated Innovation Corners showcasing La Roche-Posay’s Effaclar, Mela B3, Anthelios, Cicaplast and Lipikar ranges. Each space introduced visitors to specific skin concerns and the science behind the brand’s product formulations. Through interactive demonstrations and guided product experiences, guests gained a better understanding of different skin concerns and the role of targeted skincare in addressing them. At the Anthelios corner, visitors used a UV camera to see the effects of ultraviolet exposure and better understand the importance of sun protection. The Effaclar and Mela B3 spaces explored concerns including blemishes and hyperpigmentation, while the Cicaplast and Lipikar corners introduced visitors to approaches to caring for sensitive, damaged and dry skin. Beyond the Innovation Corners, visitors explored the Blue House, which presented La Roche-Posay’s history and commitment to dermatological innovation, and the Scars of Life Cinema. The cinema screened a 25-minute film exploring the physical and psychological realities of living with scars and scarring, including their impact on self-image and everyday life. The film also highlighted how Lipikar supports the care of skin affected by scarring, bringing attention to the importance of addressing both the visible and less visible experiences associated with skin conditions. The programme also created opportunities for visitors to engage with skincare experts and dermatologists through one-on-one consultations, ask questions about their individual skin concerns and receive guidance on building appropriate skincare routines. item.description: A historic hosting line-up spanning five African countries and a first-of-its-kind AI assistant named Infinity set the stage for a distinctive celebration as The Future Awards Africa (TFAA) marked its 20th edition on Saturday, 14 November 2026. Held at the Balmoral Convention Centre, Victoria Island, Lagos, the ceremony brought together young achievers, industry leaders and public figures to celebrate two decades of recognizing African excellence. Themed “ Celebrating the Redefiners: Africa’s AI Generation,” the evening honoured young Africans aged 18 to 35 across 26 categories, including technology and innovation, entrepreneurship, governance, music, film, literature, advocacy, sports and fashion. Their achievements formed the heart of a milestone edition that celebrated the platform’s legacy while embracing new possibilities for its stage. The event was hosted by Nigerian actress and trained lawyer Genoveva Umeh; Claudia Naisabwa , a Kenyan media personality and host; Priscilla Kayira , a Malawian radio broadcaster and television personality; Resego Motlhokathari , a television and radio host from Botswana; and Idris Sultan , a Tanzanian actor and former Big Brother Africa winner. Together, the five hosts gave the anniversary celebration a distinctly continental presence. Bringing different voices, personalities and perspectives to the proceedings, the line-up reflected the reach of an awards platform whose story has grown alongside the generations of young Africans it recognises. The hosts also shared the spotlight with Infinity , an AI assistant that introduced another dimension to the evening. With a distinct voice, quick wit, and playful responses, Infinity engaged with the hosts, drawing laughter and creating unexpected, exciting moments throughout the ceremony. Its appearance offered an exciting glimpse into how artificial intelligence is influencing not only the way people work and create, but also how audiences experience entertainment. Sharp Band and the Loud Urban Choir also entertained guests with captivating musical performances, adding to the evening’s celebratory atmosphere. At the heart of the celebration were the winners and the work that earned them recognition. Nora Awolowo received the Prize for Young Person of the Year, Teniola Aladese won the Prize for Acting, and Olamidun Ogundoyin took home the Prize for Entrepreneurship. Pastor Jerry Uchechukwu Eze , who was represented at the ceremony by media personality Hero Daniels , received the Prize for Service to Young People. The ceremony welcomed representatives of distinguished public figures, including Hon. Mobolaji Abubakre Ogunlende, Lagos State Commissioner for Youth and Social Development, who represented the Lagos State Governor, Babajide Sanwo-Olu . item.title: International Men’s Day: Six Films That Explore the Vulnerable Side of Men
item.description: One of the best aspects of art is its ability to imitate current events or imagine possibilities. Movies, as a powerful art form, present a sequence of events that allows viewers to see reflections of themselves or envision who they could become. At its core, art exists to entertain, inform and critique society. Through films, music and visual expressions, we are continually reminded of our shared humanity—our joys, flaws and contradictions. One subject that art, particularly film, has explored is masculinity. However, this theme is often addressed subtly and can be easy to overlook, as the movies that dominate global box offices frequently focus on spectacle: fantasy, romance, adventure or others. Conversations about men, their inner lives, vulnerabilities and social roles are often not in the top circle. Nonetheless, some films have attempted to explore what it means to be a man in today’s world. They invite audiences to contemplate important questions such as: What is the role of men in society? What defines a man? How does a man’s behaviour influence those around him? What expectations does society place on men? What responsibilities do men have within society? Where does responsibility begin, and where does it end? Do men matter? Do their feelings matter? The theme for this year’s International Men’s Day is “The Future Is For Everyone.” For that, here are some movies that explore and illuminate the complexities of masculinity: The Pursuit of Happyness This classic film reveals the vulnerability often hidden behind male perseverance. Will Smith ’s portrayal of Chris Gardner challenges the stoic notion of manhood by showing fatherhood as both an act of love and endurance. Through his struggles with homelessness, rejection, and exhaustion, the film redefines masculinity, depicting it as the courage to remain tender even when life tests your strength in every way. Fatherhood Kevin Hart ’s film Fatherhood delves into themes of grief and single parenthood, balancing humour with heartfelt moments. It challenges traditional expectations of masculinity by illustrating a father’s journey through uncertainty, learning empathy, and committing to being present for his child/ren. Through this film, Kevin Hart shares his vision of what it means to be a man and a father. Adolescence Adolescence examines how boys internalise distorted notions of strength and freedom, and how escaping them demands emotional awareness. The film reveals the journey of a young boy on the brink of adulthood, revealing the pressures of identity and self-definition. There is a lot to unpack from Stephen Graham’ s Adolescence about what it means to be a father and a child. King Richard A faction. In the narrative, King Richard shares the stories of Serena and Venus Williams , highlighting discipline and belief as fundamental expressions of a father’s love. The gathering brought together some of Nigeria’s leading content creators, filmmakers, advertising professionals and brand executives to explore how digital influence can translate into original intellectual property, sustainable creative businesses and longer-term commercial opportunities. Hosted by actress and media personality Bisola Aiyeola , the event gave creators a platform to present original concepts and explore new possibilities for collaboration with brands and industry stakeholders. From Content Creation to Intellectual Property A major highlight of PluggedIN 2026 was its creator showcase, featuring Taaooma, Layi Wasabi, Aproko Doctor, Ify’s Kitchen, Biodun Stephen, Osas Ighodaro, Shank Comics, Folagade Banks, Afropolitan, Bolaji Ogunmola, and Geena Foodies n Spice . The opportunity for brands lies in being part of that process through partnerships that go beyond individual sponsored posts to support the development, production and distribution of original content. For Adetutu Laditan , Creator Economy Catalyst and Founder of Woof Studios Africa, this shift requires a more structured approach to supporting creators and connecting them with the right opportunities. “Our vision at Woof Studios Africa has always been to empower African creators to move beyond virality and build lasting, profitable enterprises. Nigerian creators are thinking bigger, and forward-thinking brands want to be part of that evolution,” she said. Laditan explained that Woof Studios works across the business and production aspects of content development, including funding and distribution, to help creators take ideas beyond their initial digital formats. “When creators understand a brand’s business objectives, and brands respect the authentic voice a creator has spent years cultivating, we stop simply buying attention and start co-creating stories that matter.” The conversations at PluggedIN also addressed the realities of building sustainable creative businesses. During the creator-focused panel, Kiekie, Craze Clown, Jay On-Air and Winifred Nwania of Zeelicious Food discussed the opportunities and challenges of building careers in the digital space. They explored content ownership, audience engagement, monetisation and the importance of meaningful brand relationships. The discussions reflected an increasingly important question for the industry: How can creators turn the audiences and cultural influence they have built into sustainable businesses? item.title: Ibukun Awosika, Juliet Ibrahim, Bola Adesola & More: Leading Women Take Centre Stage at The Executive Woman Summit 2.0
item.description: What does it really mean to play to win in business and leadership? Beyond earning a seat at the table, it requires more than competence or professional accomplishments. It requires the confidence to own one’s value, the clarity to communicate one’s contributions and the intentionality to build visibility that translates into meaningful influence. These conversations defined The Executive Woman Summit (TEWS) 2.0 , which brought together hundreds of executive women, corporate professionals, entrepreneurs and emerging leaders at Harbour Point, Victoria Island, Lagos, on Wednesday, October 28, 2026. Convened by Bola Matel-Okoh , a dual-qualified attorney (called to both the New York and Nigerian Bars), Executive Coach, Non-Executive Director at Wema Bank, and CEO of BMO Advisory Services , the second edition of the summit was themed Playing to Win: Elevate Your Vision, Value and Visibility. It provided an intentional platform for candid conversations, practical insights and strategic alliances on what it takes for women to advance, lead and thrive in today’s evolving corporate landscape. In her opening address, Matel-Okoh challenged women to rethink how they approach professional visibility, authority and advancement. According to her, competence is merely the baseline; it is not enough if you are unwilling to communicate your value, own your voice and position yourself for higher-stakes opportunities. This philosophy also came through in her cover interview with THISDAY Glitterati ahead of the summit, where she offered a compelling perspective on the distinction between holding a powerful position and exercising genuine influence. “A powerful position gives you formal authority. Influence determines how deeply your leadership shapes people’s thinking, decisions and actions. A title may secure your place in a meeting, but credibility makes people listen,” she explained. She also challenged the assumption that excellent work will automatically speak for itself, encouraging women to communicate their contributions with evidence and confidence. “What problem did you solve? What result did you produce? What changed because of your leadership?” she asked, highlighting the importance of making professional value visible to the decision-makers who influence career progression and boardroom opportunities. “There is no need to diminish your achievements to make others comfortable. You can be gracious and still be clear about the value you bring,” she added. The summit featured a distinguished line-up of women shaping leadership, business, finance, entertainment and corporate governance. Chairman of Ecobank Nigeria, Bola Adesola , and CEO of FS Global Advisory Services, Folake Sanu , delivered keynote addresses, sharing perspectives on leadership, professional growth, boardroom dynamics and navigating the demands of executive life.
